analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 estate tax repeal permanent instead of letting it expire after 2010.
analysis.headline: The House passed permanent estate tax repeal 256-171 on June 6, 2002, but the Senate never voted, so the estate tax repeal kept its scheduled expiration.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law phased out the federal estate tax but included a built-in expiration date, so the tax was set to come back after 2010. This bill struck that expiration date, making the repeal permanent. Because the House passed it in June 2002 but the Senate never took it up before that Congress ended, the sunset stayed in place.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs to the largest estates. The estate tax only applies to estates above a size threshold, which in 2001 law rose to $3.5 million per couple by 2009 before repeal, so only a small share of the wealthiest families would owe it. Supporters also argued it spared family farms and small businesses from selling assets to pay the tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the sunset provision in the 2001 tax cut law that applied to the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax title, so the repeal would not expire after 2010.
It makes the change retroactive in effect, treating the repeal of the sunset as if it had been part of the original 2001 law.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury. Estate tax revenue — paid by the largest estates — would disappear permanently, meaning the money either comes from other taxpayers, from government services, or from borrowing.

drawbacks.text: The repeal has no offset: permanent repeal permanently removes revenue that comes only from the largest estates, meaning the cost falls on the budget that funds everything else or on future taxpayers through borrowing.

Opponents in the House tried to require that any tax reduction in the bill be contingent on not using Social Security surpluses, arguing the tax cut would draw on those funds; the House rejected that condition.
The sunset provision in the 2001 law existed to keep the tax cut within budget rules; striking it removes the mechanism designed to limit the cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes almost entirely to a small group of very wealthy families, since the estate tax at its 2009 level would touch only the largest estates. The cost — tens of billions per year once fully phased in — is spread across every federal taxpayer and program. Supporters' farm and small-business arguments address a real concern, but the exemption increases in the 2001 law already spared most of those estates before repeal fully took effect.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on June 6, 2002, but the Senate just placed it on its calendar and never voted before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced June 12, 2001, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it sat for nearly a year.
The House Rules Committee set up floor consideration with a rule allowing one hour of debate and a specified amendment, and the House adopted the rule on June 6, 2002.

Democrats offered a motion to send the bill back to committee with instructions to add a provision making the tax cut contingent on not using Social Security funds; it failed 205-223, with 203 of 211 voting Democrats in favor and 217 of 222 Republicans opposed.
The House passed the bill 256-171, with 214 of 222 Republicans and 41 of 211 Democrats in favor.
The Senate received the bill, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders on June 10, 2002, where it remained until the Congress ended without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the Senate never acted, the federal treasury kept estate tax revenue that permanent repeal would have eliminated, and the wealthiest estates remained subject to the tax rather than gaining a permanent repeal.

for.name: Dave Weldon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2001 estate tax repeal permanent.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee
for.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Bill Thomas, R-CA)
for.what_they_did: Held jurisdiction over the bill; it came to the floor under a rule in June 2002 after sitting in committee for nearly a year.

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Pushed Congress to make the 2001 tax cuts, including estate tax repeal, permanent.

against.name: 205 House members (203 of 211 voting Democrats)
against.role: Blok that supported the motion to recommit
against.what_they_did: Voted to send the bill back to committee with instructions to make the tax cut contingent on not raiding Social Security funds; the motion failed 205-223.

against.name: Tom Daschle
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate vote; it stayed on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split sharply by party — 214 of 222 Republicans yes, 41 of 211 Democrats yes — though 41 Democrats crossed over to pass it 256-171; the Senate, where Democrats held a working majority, never voted.

industries.note: The estate tax falls only on estates above a size threshold, so permanent repeal is a direct transfer of value to the largest family fortunes, paid for out of general federal revenue. The bill's passage would have locked that in before repeal fully took effect.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and trust/wealth management firms
industries.note: A large industry of lawyers, accountants, and advisers exists around estate tax planning; permanent repeal would shrink that demand. Their loss runs alongside, not against, families avoiding the tax.
A common product is insurance bought to cover expected estate tax bills; repeal removes the need for it. Ordinary policyholders are not directly affected either way.
